analysis.one_liner: Repeals Clean Air Act rules requiring cleaner-burning gasoline and employer programs to cut employee driving.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee after referral in early 1995, and the Clean Air Act's reformulated gasoline and employer trip-reduction rules remained in force.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have deleted two sections of the Clean Air Act. One required oil refiners to sell specially blended, cleaner-burning gasoline in the cities with the worst smog; the other required employers in severely polluted areas to run programs getting workers to carpool, take transit, or otherwise drive fewer solo trips. Repealing both would have cut compliance costs for refiners and paperwork for large employers, but would have allowed more smog in the most polluted metropolitan areas.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil refiners and fuel sellers in smoggy metro areas, who would no longer have to produce and stock specially blended reformulated gasoline; large employers in severe ozone nonattainment areas, who would no longer have to run employee commute-reduction programs; and drivers in those areas, who would no longer be required to buy the pricier blended fuel.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 211(k) of the Clean Air Act, ending the federal requirement that cleaner-burning reformulated gasoline be sold in specified smoggy areas, freeing refiners and fuel sellers of that obligation.
Repeals the employer trip-reduction mandate for severe ozone areas, ending the requirement that employers in those areas adopt plans to cut work-related vehicle trips by their employees.
Drivers and consumers in covered areas could buy ordinary (cheaper) gasoline again instead of the mandated reformulated blend.

analysis.who_pays: People who live and breathe in the affected smoggy metropolitan areas, who would face dirtier air and the health risks that come with it, and the state and local air-quality programs that would lose two mandated tools for meeting federal smog standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents of areas with smog problems

drawbacks.text: Repeal would have removed a mandated cleaner-burning fuel from the markets with the worst ozone pollution, allowing more smog and its associated respiratory health risks in exactly the areas that already failed federal air standards.
It would have deleted employer-based trip-reduction programs — one of the few tools in the law aimed at reducing total vehicle miles in severe smog areas — before any replacement existed.

The bill repealed the programs outright rather than reforming them, so even employers and communities that wanted flexibility would have gotten no middle ground, and air-quality plans built around these requirements would have been upended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings are real but private and modest: lower fuel-blending compliance costs for refiners and less administrative burden for employers. The costs are diffuse but broad: more smog in the nation's most polluted metro areas and a weaker federal backstop for air quality. On balance the costs to public health outweigh the savings, and the repeal-all approach left no room for the flexibility critics of the original mandates wanted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, which never took it up, so it quietly died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Neumann introduced the bill on February 24, 1995, joined by Reps. Sensenbrenner and Petri.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Commerce.
On March 3, 1995, it was referred again to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action was ever recorded — no markup, no floor vote — before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the Clean Air Act provisions it targeted stayed on the books.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Residents of smoggy metropolitan areas came out ahead, because the reformulated gasoline and employer trip-reduction requirements remained in force; refiners and large employers kept bearing the compliance costs the bill would have lifted.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Environment

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly all Republican: the sponsor and 5 of the 6 cosponsors were Republicans, with a single Democratic cosponsor, and the bill never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: The reformulated gasoline program required refiners to produce and sell a specially blended, cleaner-burning fuel in the worst-smog cities. Repealing it would have ended that compliance cost — but the savings came from putting a dirtier fuel back into exactly the markets with the worst air.

industries.industry: Large employers in severe ozone nonattainment areas
industries.note: Federal law required employers in severely polluted areas to adopt plans cutting employees' solo work trips. Repeal would have ended that mandate, relieving employers of program costs while giving up commute-related emission reductions.

Reformulated gasoline rules guaranteed a market for fuel oxygenates, of which ethanol was a major Midwest supplier; repealing the program would have erased that guaranteed demand. Their loss was tied to the pollution-control program rather than to cleaner or dirtier fuel on its own terms.
